archetype.name: Rebuilding (three-and-free-throw offense)
archetype.definition: A team in year three of a slide, still losing by a wide margin. It leans on two veteran scorers while a young backcourt, half of it currently out, learns on the job.

report.headline: The defense has stopped the bleeding; the offense is now the bigger problem.
report.take:
Brooklyn at 2-8 is about what its margin says it is. W vs Pt Diff sits at 0, and the differential implies exactly 2 wins. There is no bad luck to wait out. The Net Rtg of -9 ranks 24th and the offense ranks 28th. History says this is no blip: the record has gone from 32-50 to 26-56 to 20-62 over the last three years. The current pace of 16 wins points to a similar finish. On the site's Teams tab the Nets come in 20th of 30, kinder than the record but still firmly in the bottom third.

The shape of the team has shifted, though. Last season's defense ranked 26th with a 119.0 DRtg. This one is at 115.4, 19th, and in November it allowed 110.2 a game against 121.2 in October. It rebounds its own glass well, with a DRB % of 74.9 that ranks 5th. It has been stingy against point guards, allowing 20.5 points a game to the position, 2nd fewest. The hole is at the rim. Opponents shoot 70.8% within four feet, 27th in the league and well above the league's 65.2%. Wings and forwards also take a bigger share of the scoring against Brooklyn than they do league-wide.

The offense is where the losing comes from. It runs on two ideas that work: a 3PA Rate of 48 (4th) and an FT Rate of 33.5 (5th), both up on last year. Then it gives the gains back. The TOV % of 15.9 ranks 28th, worse than last year's 14.3. The ORB % of 25.5 ranks 24th, and the 3P % of 34.4 is merely league average. Michael Porter Jr. (215 points, 60.0 TS %) and Julius Randle (200 points) carry the scoring. Nolan Traoré has been the real find: 62.4 TS %, a 2.3 BPM, 17th of 83 on the point guard tab. Beyond those three the shooting falls away. Keon Ellis is at 41.7 TS % and Chaney Johnson at 46.7.

The on-off splits explain a lot of the night-to-night swings, with one caveat: ten games of lineup data are noisy. The team has been far better with Day'Ron Sharpe on the floor (+17.8) and far worse with Noah Clowney (-14.0) or Moritz Wagner (-15.5). Wagner's 67.6 TS % says his scoring isn't the issue, which points to the defensive end. Mikel Brown Jr. and Egor Dëmin are both out, and the backcourt grades D-. The likely path is more of the same: a bad team showing signs of a better defense, without the shot-making to turn that into wins.

strengths.title: Threes and free throws
strengths.body: Brooklyn builds its shot diet the modern way: nearly half its attempts come from three and it gets to the line at a top-five rate. Both rates are up on last season's, so this looks like a deliberate plan rather than noise. It is what keeps a 28th-ranked offense from being even worse, and it should hold.

strengths.title: A defense climbing out of the cellar
strengths.body: The DRtg of 115.4 is a clear step up from last year's 119.0. November allowed 110.2 a game, and the last five games have been 5.5 points a game stingier than the season average. Defensive rebounding (5th in DRB %) and point-guard containment are doing the work. Some of November's number comes from soft scoring nights by Indiana and Charlotte, but the improvement looks partly real.

strengths.title: Traoré as a real building block
strengths.body: The young point guard is scoring efficiently at a 62.4 TS % on 23% usage and grades 17th of 83 at his position. He is the only backcourt player with a positive BPM. With Brown Jr. and Dëmin out, his development is the most important thing happening on this roster.

concerns.title: Turnovers sink the offense
concerns.body: A TOV % of 15.9 ranks 28th and is 2.1 above the league average. It wipes out the gains from the shot profile, and it is worse than last season. A backcourt this young and thin, with two guards out, is unlikely to fix it quickly. Paired with weak offensive rebounding, it leaves the Nets with too few good shots.

concerns.title: No rim protection
concerns.body: Brooklyn doesn't give up an unusual share of rim attempts, but opponents finish them at 70.8%, 27th in the league. The center rotation is split between Sharpe, who has helped, and Wagner, who has not by on-off. Unless Sharpe's minutes grow, this is structural.

concerns.title: Thin, injured backcourt
concerns.body: The backcourt grades D-, and two of its four listed guards are out. Ellis is shooting a 41.7 TS % in heavy minutes. That forces Porter and Randle to create more than they should, and the turnover numbers show the strain.

trend.note: An 0-5 October that included one-score losses at Cleveland and Boston became a 2-3 November. The defense got better while the offense slid to 103.2 a game, and the 37-point loss at Dallas shows the floor hasn't really moved.

weekAhead.headline: Two road games and a strong Philly defense: likely one win, maybe none
weekAhead.body:
The week opens in New Orleans against the most beatable opponent. The Pelicans' defense is 21st by DRtg, and their rim protection is as leaky as Brooklyn's. Both teams will attack the paint: the Pelicans rank 30th in 3PA Rate and 3rd in FT Rate, a direct test of the Nets' 27th-ranked rim defense. Memphis is the best team on the slate at 8th on the site, with a +6.1 Net Rtg and a league-leading rebounding team. The trip home brings Philadelphia, 9-2 but only 14th by Net Rtg, with a top-five defense.

The realistic target is one win, and New Orleans is the obvious spot. The Philadelphia game is better than the 76ers' record suggests, since their record is running ahead of their margin. Their elite three-point defense is bad news for a team that lives behind the arc.

keyMatchups.title: Randle and Traoré against New Orleans
keyMatchups.body: New Orleans gives up 26.7 points a game to power forwards, 27th in the league and well above those players' own averages. Point guards score 31.9 a game on them, also 27th. Randle and Traoré get the softest spots on the floor. Porter does not: the Pelicans allow only 15.8 a game to small forwards, 2nd fewest, so the offense should run through the other two.

keyMatchups.title: The glass in Memphis
keyMatchups.body: Memphis leads the league in RPG and ranks 2nd in REB %. Brooklyn's one rebounding strength is its defensive boards, and that is exactly where this game will be decided. The Grizzlies force few turnovers, ranking 23rd in Opp TOV %, which gives the Nets' turnover problem some room to breathe.

keyMatchups.title: Threes against Philadelphia's perimeter defense
keyMatchups.body: Philadelphia holds opponents to 31.6% from three, 2nd best, and leads the league in W vs Pt Diff, so its record is partly close-game luck. The opening is inside: the 76ers allow the 2nd-highest share of shots at the rim. Brooklyn would do well to trade some threes for drives and free throws.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Brooklyn can protect the rim against a New Orleans team built to get there and to the line. That game is the Nets' best chance at a win this week.

restOfSeason.body:
Nothing in the margin suggests a turnaround. The record and the differential agree, and the three-year trend runs one way. The defensive gains look partly real, given the rebounding and the point-guard containment, and that should keep this from being a repeat of last season's bottom-two finish. The offense is the cap. Turnovers, poor offensive rebounding and a shallow pool of efficient shooters beyond Porter, Randle and Traoré don't fix themselves mid-season. Something like 17-24 wins, with a Net Rtg between roughly -10 and -6, is the honest range.

The upside case runs through health and growth in the backcourt. Brown Jr. and Dëmin could return and cut the turnover rate, Traoré could hold his efficiency, and Sharpe could take more of the center minutes. The downside case is that the veteran scorers' production fades, and in a rebuild their minutes may not stay stable.
swingFactors: Brown Jr. and Dëmin's return and the turnover rate
Sharpe's share of the center minutes
Whether Porter and Randle keep their minutes and efficiency

confidence.note: Only 10 games, but record, margin and a three-year history all point the same way.
